title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem #214 (1983, SOLVED): If S ⊂ ℝ² has no two points at distance 1, must the complement Sᶜ contain four points forming a unit square? YES — Juhász (1979) proved the complement must contain a congruent copy of ANY 4-point configuration, not just squares.
mathContext: The problem concerns the geometric Ramsey theory of the plane: partitioning $\mathbb{R}^2$ into $S$ and $S^c$ where $S$ avoids unit distances forces $S^c$ to be geometrically rich. The result is equivalent to: the unit distance graph $G_1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ has the property that every independent set has a complement containing all 4-point configurations up to congruence.

title: Plane and Distance
content: The Euclidean plane ℝ² is defined as EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2), and distance as ‖p - q‖. This uses Mathlib's inner product space structure on ℝ^n.
mathContext: The plane $\mathbb{R}^2 = \texttt{EuclideanSpace}\;\mathbb{R}\;(\texttt{Fin } 2)$ has the Euclidean norm $\|p - q\| = \sqrt{(p_0 - q_0)^2 + (p_1 - q_1)^2}$. The $\texttt{dist}$ function wraps this norm. All distance-based definitions use this metric.

title: IsUnitDistanceFree
content: A set S ⊆ ℝ² is unit-distance-free if no two distinct points in S are exactly distance 1 apart: ∀ p, q ∈ S, p ≠ q → ‖p - q‖ ≠ 1. Equivalently, S is an independent set in the unit distance graph.
mathContext: $\texttt{IsUnitDistanceFree}(S) \iff \forall p, q \in S,\; p \neq q \implies \|p - q\| \neq 1$. Such sets are precisely the independent sets of the unit distance graph $G_1(\mathbb{R}^2)$. The maximum density of such a set is related to $1/\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$, where $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2) \in \{5, 6, 7\}$ is the chromatic number of the plane.

title: IsUnitSquare and ContainsUnitSquare
content: Four points form a unit square if all four edges have length 1 and both diagonals have length √2. ContainsUnitSquare(S) means S contains four such points. The side-diagonal characterization uniquely determines a square up to congruence.
mathContext: The conditions $d(p_i, p_{i+1}) = 1$ for edges and $d(p_1, p_3) = d(p_2, p_4) = \sqrt{2}$ characterize a unit square. The diagonal condition $d = \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}$ follows from the Pythagorean theorem for a square with side 1. Note: the ordering $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4$ traces the perimeter, so the definition checks a specific labeling of the square's vertices.

title: Erdos214Statement and Solution
content: The main statement: ∀ S, IsUnitDistanceFree S → ContainsUnitSquare Sᶜ. Juhász's theorem (1979) is axiomatized as juhasz_1979, and erdos_214_solved simply applies it. The complement Sᶜ must contain a unit square whenever S avoids the unit distance.
mathContext: $\texttt{Erdos214Statement} = \forall S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,\; \texttt{IsUnitDistanceFree}(S) \to \texttt{ContainsUnitSquare}(S^c)$. Juhász's proof uses the fact that for any $p \in S$, the entire unit circle $\{q : \|p - q\| = 1\}$ lies in $S^c$. With enough unit circles in $S^c$, their intersection patterns guarantee the existence of four points forming a unit square.

title: Juhász's Stronger Theorem — Any 4-Point Set
content: Juhász proved a stronger result: the complement contains a congruent copy of ANY 4-point configuration, not just unit squares. ContainsCongruentCopy uses an isometry f with f(P_i) ∈ Sᶜ for all i. The theorem unit_square_from_stronger derives the original statement (sorry: needs explicit unit square as PointSet 4).
mathContext: $\texttt{JuhaszStrongerTheorem} = \forall S,\; \texttt{IsUnitDistanceFree}(S) \to \forall P : \texttt{Fin } 4 \to \mathbb{R}^2,\; \exists f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ isometry with $f(P_i) \in S^c\; \forall i$. The isometry preserves all distances, so the image is congruent to $P$. This is a Ramsey-type theorem: avoiding one distance (unit) in $S$ forces ALL bounded configurations in $S^c$. The 4-point threshold is sharp — the result fails for some $n$-point configurations when $n$ is large enough.

title: Limitations and the 5-Point Question
content: The result fails for sufficiently large n-point configurations: ∃ n, ∃ S unit-distance-free with ∃ P (n-point set) not congruently embedded in Sᶜ. The 5-point case is formalized as HoldsFor5Points : Prop and remains OPEN.
mathContext: The failure for large $n$ is expected: a unit-distance-free $S$ can have positive (Lebesgue) measure (e.g., a union of small disks), and for large $n$, some $n$-point configurations require more 'room' than $S^c$ provides locally. The critical threshold — the largest $n$ for which the property holds for ALL $n$-point configurations — is unknown. The 5-point case is the first open instance.

title: Unit Distance Graph and Chromatic Number
content: Defines UnitDistanceGraph(S) = {(p,q) : p,q ∈ S, p≠q, dist(p,q)=1}. Proves unit_distance_free_iff_no_edges: S is unit-distance-free iff its unit distance graph is empty. Also states the chromatic number χ(ℝ²) ∈ {5,6,7} (de Grey 2018 lower bound).
mathContext: The theorem $\texttt{unit\_distance\_free\_iff\_no\_edges}$ is fully proved: ($\to$) if $S$ is unit-distance-free and $(p,q) \in \texttt{UDG}(S)$, then $p, q \in S$ with $\|p-q\| = 1$, contradicting the definition; ($\leftarrow$) if $\texttt{UDG}(S) = \emptyset$ and $p, q \in S$ with $\|p-q\| = 1$, then $(p,q) \in \texttt{UDG}(S) = \emptyset$, contradiction. The chromatic number $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$ connects: each color class in a proper coloring is unit-distance-free, so Juhász's theorem applies to each class.

title: Proof Techniques (Placeholder Axioms)
content: Three placeholder axioms (True) sketch the proof strategy: (1) maximal unit-distance-free sets have specific geometric structure, (2) for any p ∈ S, the unit circle at p lies in Sᶜ (pigeonhole), (3) unit circles intersect in ≤ 2 points, limiting local sparseness of Sᶜ.
mathContext: The key geometric insight: for $p \in S$, the circle $\{q : \|p-q\| = 1\}$ lies entirely in $S^c$ (since $q \in S$ would give a unit distance pair). For two points $p_1, p_2 \in S$ with $\|p_1 - p_2\| \neq 1$, their unit circles intersect in $\leq 2$ points. The intersection points, together with the circle arcs in $S^c$, provide enough points to construct any 4-point configuration. The proof uses a continuity/compactness argument on the configuration space.

title: Examples: Scaled Lattice
content: The integer lattice ℤ² is NOT unit-distance-free (contains (0,0) and (1,0) at distance 1). The scaled lattice √2·ℤ² IS unit-distance-free (axiomatized), and its complement contains unit squares (axiomatized). The scaling factor √2 ensures no lattice pair has distance 1.
mathContext: For the scaled lattice $\sqrt{2}\mathbb{Z}^2$: two points $(\sqrt{2}a, \sqrt{2}b)$ and $(\sqrt{2}c, \sqrt{2}d)$ have distance $\sqrt{2}\sqrt{(a-c)^2 + (b-d)^2}$. This equals 1 iff $(a-c)^2 + (b-d)^2 = 1/2$, which has no integer solutions. So the lattice is unit-distance-free. Its complement is 'most of $\mathbb{R}^2$' (Lebesgue measure 1), making it easy to find unit squares there.
